title: The Pathetic Life of Wagie: A Critique of Predatorial Capitalism & Worker Alienation
summary: A narrated essay reading Kengan Ashura as a critique of predatory capitalism and worker alienation, centred on the salaryman Yamashita Kazuo. NH explains how corporate hierarchies grind down employees, why regulating capitalism is close to impossible, and concludes that personal refusal works for a story but is not realistic for most people.
claims: What makes a fighting manga special is how it justifies its fights; beneath the tournament battles, Kengan Ashura is a social critique of capitalism and worker alienation
The average Japanese salaryman spends 10 to 14 hours a day at work under a boss's power and bows to keep his livelihood even when he has done nothing wrong

Capitalism is simply competition inside organised society when the state does not control it, which makes it a natural human drive; what is unnatural is the global scale that has turned corporations and their billionaire owners into new gods

Worker alienation unfolds in stages: you drift into a job without passion to pay the bills, it takes over your identity, then the dissonance of a job that both sustains you and makes you miserable pushes you into coping with alcohol and hedonism
Employment trades freedom for material comfort that then makes you dependent; whatever you own, you really owe to the company or the bank
Big companies dominate governments as much as their workers, and toppling one corporate tyrant only makes room for the next
Some people are dominated because they allow it; predators who refuse slave morality become the masters, which is what makes capitalism so ruthless
Regulating markets would mean micromanaging an entire anthill and would take total financial control or military force, which only totalitarian states have
In Kengan Ashura the salaryman escapes alienation by refusing to play the game, but NH thinks simply quitting is not realistic for most people
Liberation will not come from one-on-one relationships; it has to start with one person's fortitude spreading until the one becomes the many
